digest.top_line: AGITG MASTERPLAN: SBRT 40Gy/5fx added to induction CT cut 12mth LRR to 20.2% vs 52.0% (p=0.022), with mOS 22.0 vs 14.0mo, in a randomised phase II.
digest.tldr: Upper-GI carried the day with opposite signals. Adding SBRT to induction CT improved LRR and OS in MASTERPLAN, while adding IO to dCRT stayed null in locally advanced esophageal/GEJ cancer (KEYNOTE-975 EFS HR 0.97 in CPS ≥10; ARION cPFS HR 0.91). In bone mets, PALEM embolization met both co-primaries, and FURTHER (MR-HIFU) missed its primary on 69 of 129 pts.

sites.intro: Two options for painful bone mets: embolization when RT is not an option or has already been given (PALEM), and MR-HIFU ± EBRT (FURTHER, underpowered).

studies.name: FURTHER
studies.tldr: 2-week pain response 50% vs 38% for MR-HIFU ± EBRT vs EBRT alone (p=0.41) in painful non-spinal bone mets; underpowered, N=69 of 129 target.
details: 📊 Primary endpoint not met: 2-wk pain response 50% (MR-HIFU ± EBRT pooled) vs 38% EBRT, p = 0.41
🔍 Multicenter RCT, 6 European hospitals, 1:1:1 randomization, enrolled 2020-2025
🔍 Arms: MR-HIFU (n=22), EBRT followed by MR-HIFU within 1 wk (n=23), EBRT (n=24)
⚠️ Accrual 69 vs target 129 despite 2-yr extension (COVID-19, low MR-HIFU eligibility)
⚠️ Primary comparison pools two HIFU arms vs EBRT, diluting the combination signal
⚠️ EBRT dose/fractionation not reported in source
⚠️ 81% combination response is secondary and unpowered; Bayesian reanalysis pending
🔍 Excluded: spinal mets, life expectancy <3 mo, (impending) fracture, curative intent

verdict.rationale: Accrued 69 of 129 planned; null pooled primary. Positive read rests on unpowered secondary arm-level data, so neither superiority nor equivalence to EBRT is established.
verdict.audience: Painful (NRS ≥4) non-spinal bone mets, EBRT-eligible, no fracture

studies.significance: The RT-relevant signal sits in the secondary data: EBRT followed by MR-HIFU reached 81% pain response by wk 6 vs 47% for EBRT alone, against a background expectation of 70%. EBRT dose is not reported in source, so whether this adds to single-fraction practice cannot be judged; it frames HIFU as an adjunct question, not a replacement.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with painful non-spinal bone mets who has exhausted EBRT options, this supports MR-HIFU as a palliative alternative; it does not support replacing EBRT in the RT-eligible pt.

primary_endpoint.name: Pain response 2 weeks after start of treatment
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: MR-HIFU ± EBRT vs EBRT; p = 0.41, not significant

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicenter RCT across **six European hospitals**, 1:1:1 randomization, enrolled 2020-2025. **69 randomized** against a target of **129**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adults with good/reasonable performance and **painful (NRS ≥ 4) non-spinal bone metastases** eligible for both EBRT and MR-HIFU. Excluded life expectancy <3 months, (impending) fracture, or curative intent.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: MR-HIFU alone, EBRT alone, or EBRT followed by MR-HIFU within one week. EBRT dose and fractionation not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** pain response at 2 weeks from start of treatment, by Brief Pain Inventory pain score and opioid use. Secondary: pain scores and pain response over the first three months.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Pooled MR-HIFU arms vs EBRT at 2 weeks: **50% vs. 38%, p = 0.41**. Arm-level secondary data shown in the table.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents EBRT-eligible pts with painful non-spinal bone metastases and no fracture risk. Does not represent spinal metastases, (impending) fracture, or life expectancy <3 months.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EBRT remains the standard, with the source citing **70%** pain response and onset over 4-6 weeks. FURTHER does not show MR-HIFU beats that standard at its 2-week primary timepoint.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Pooling both HIFU arms into the primary comparison mixes a monotherapy and an adjunct question. Eligibility for MR-HIFU proved lower than expected, so the trial population is a selected subset of bone-met referrals.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The combination arm's late rise is hypothesis-generating for HIFU as an EBRT adjunct, not a substitute. Whether the planned Bayesian analysis changes the read is not settled by this abstract.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The arm-level secondaries favor EBRT followed by MR-HIFU (81% response by wk 6 vs 47% EBRT alone), but the trial was powered for none of this. EBRT dose is not reported in source, so it does not yet inform fractionation choice; MR-HIFU is best read as an option when EBRT is no longer available.

open_questions: Does EBRT plus MR-HIFU beat EBRT alone in an adequately powered trial?
Durability of MR-HIFU pain response beyond three months
Does Bayesian reanalysis change the primary read?

studies.name: PALEM
studies.tldr: Arterial embolization gave immediate pain relief in 52.5% (95% CI 43.1-61.8%) of RT-ineligible or post-RT painful bone mets at 72 h; no primary safety events.
details: 🔍 Multicenter, single-arm, prospective confirmatory hypothesis-testing study under J-SUPPORT palliative trial standards
🔍 N=120 enrolled; 118 evaluable for efficacy, 119 in safety set

subdetails: RT-ineligible, or ≥8 weeks after prior RT

details: 💊 Microsphere embolization of tumor-feeding vessels, no anticancer drug in the embolic

details.text: 📊 Co-primary endpoints vs prespecified thresholds (both met)

rows: Embolization-related G≥4 AE or G≥3 CNS necrosis to day 14

details: 📐 Efficacy: one-sided α=0.025, power 0.9, assumed 40% response
🔗 Response borrowed international consensus criteria for palliative RT trials (pain score + morphine-equivalent dose), BPI-SF item 3
⚠️ Efficacy counts any pain reduction; the abstract gives no minimum point drop
⚠️ Safety endpoint captures only G≥4 or G≥3 CNS necrosis; lower-grade AEs not reported in source
⚠️ Single 72 h read; durability, retreatment and re-intervention rates not reported

verdict.rationale: Single-arm design caps it despite prespecified hypothesis testing; no comparator vs palliative RT or re-irradiation, 72 h endpoint only.
verdict.audience: Painful bone mets, pain ≥5 on analgesics, RT-ineligible or ≥8 wk post-RT

studies.significance: Eligibility excluded RT candidates (RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks post-RT), and response used the palliative RT consensus criteria read at 72 h. That makes embolization an option for the already-irradiated or unirradiable painful lesion, not a competitor to first-course palliative RT, which it was never compared against.
studies.monday_clinic: In a painful bone metastasis already irradiated ≥8 weeks ago or deemed RT-ineligible, this supports arterial embolization as a rapid-relief option; it does not inform the RT-naive lesion, where it was never compared with palliative RT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicenter, **single-arm**, prospective confirmatory hypothesis-testing study under J-SUPPORT palliative standards; protocol published. **N=120** enrolled. UMIN000040794.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Painful bone metastases on analgesics with **pain score ≥5**, and either **RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks after prior RT**. Only the most painful lesion was embolized.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Arterial embolization of tumor-feeding vessels with **microspheres**, with no anticancer drug in the embolic.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Co-primary:** immediate efficacy at 72 h (BPI-SF item 3 plus daily morphine-equivalent dose, per palliative RT consensus criteria) and safety through day 14. Overall success required **both**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Efficacy in **62/118 (52.5%, 95% CI 43.1-61.8%)**, clearing the 26% null. **No primary safety events** in 119 (95% CI 0.0-3.1%) against a <15% bound.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: The safety endpoint counted only embolization-related **grade ≥4 events or grade ≥3 CNS necrosis**. Lower-grade toxicity, including post-embolization pain, is not reported in the source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Palliative RT is the standard for painful bone metastases, and this trial deliberately took its response definition from the palliative RT consensus criteria. It enrolled pts outside that standard (RT-ineligible or post-RT), so it **does not test embolization against RT**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents painful bone metastases with pain ≥5 on analgesics that are RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks past prior RT. Does not represent RT-naive lesions eligible for first-course palliative RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Response counts any pain reduction, or stable pain with an opioid reduction, without a stated minimum change. A single 72 h timepoint says nothing about durability, and the narrow safety definition leaves the full AE profile unreported.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The trial shows that a measurable share of refractory pts get pain relief within days, where analgesics are otherwise the only option. Whether that relief lasts, and how it compares with re-irradiation, remain open.

studies.interpretation:
The design choice that matters most for a radiation oncologist is who was allowed in. PALEM did not enroll pts who would ordinarily get palliative RT. Eligibility required RT-ineligibility or at least 8 weeks since prior RT, so the population is the lesion that has already been irradiated and still hurts, or one where RT is off the table for anatomic or logistic reasons. Read that way, the result does not compete with first-course palliative RT. It addresses the gap after it, where the realistic alternatives are re-irradiation, escalating opioids, or nothing.

Borrowing the international consensus response criteria for palliative RT trials helps and hurts. It helps because the composite of pain score and morphine-equivalent dose is familiar, and it stops opioid escalation from passing as success. It hurts because the abstract's version is lenient: any reduction in pain score with stable or falling opioids counts, as does stable pain with less opioid, and no minimum point change is stated. A 52.5% response rate under that definition is not obviously comparable to RT response rates built on stricter thresholds, and a reader should not set the two side by side. The 72 h timepoint fits the claimed advantage, speed, but it is also the window most open to placebo and procedural effects in an unblinded single-arm study.

The statistics are tidy. The trial was powered against a 26% null with a 40% expected response, and the observed lower confidence bound of 43.1% clears that comfortably. A single-arm confirmatory design can show that embolization beats a fixed historical floor. It cannot show that embolization beats re-irradiation or optimized analgesia in the same pts, and that is the comparison a tumor board needs.

The safety result rests on a deliberately narrow endpoint. No grade 4 events or grade 3 CNS necrosis in 119 pts is reassuring about catastrophic non-target embolization, especially near the spine. It says nothing about grade 1 to 3 events such as post-embolization pain, fever, or skin and muscle ischemia, which drive the pt's experience in the first week. The full paper needs to report those.

What would change the read is durability. Embolization devascularizes tumor and does not address the cause of bone pain the way RT does over weeks. If relief fades by one to three months, the procedure is most useful as a bridge, for example to cover the delay before re-irradiation takes effect, or for pts with very short expected survival. If relief lasts, it becomes a real alternative in the post-RT setting. Neither possibility can be told apart from a 72 h endpoint.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Eligibility excluded RT candidates (RT-ineligible or ≥8 weeks post-RT), so embolization enters as an option for the previously irradiated painful lesion, alongside re-irradiation, not instead of first-course palliative RT. Response used the palliative RT consensus criteria at 72 h, with no head-to-head data against RT.

open_questions: Durability of pain relief beyond 72 h
Embolization vs re-irradiation for post-RT painful bone mets
Embolization as bridge to or combined with palliative RT

sites.intro: Two trials found no benefit from adding concurrent IO to dCRT in esophageal cancer (KEYNOTE-975 phase 3 stopped, ARION phase II), while local SBRT showed benefit in MASTERPLAN.

studies.name: ARION PRODIGE 67
studies.tldr: Durvalumab + dCRT did not improve 12-mo cPFS (48.6% vs 48.9%, HR 0.91) in locally advanced esophageal cancer.
details: 🔍 Open-label comparative phase II, N=112 randomized (58 vs 54), 13 French sites
🔍 Stratified by tumor stage, histology, center
📐 Powered for HR 0.55 (74 cPFS events, 90% power, 10% one-sided alpha)

details.text: 📊 Efficacy at 24-mo follow-up analysis, SoC + D vs SoC

subdetails: RT: IMRT 50 Gy/25 daily fx over 5 wk, both arms
Chemo: FOLFOX x6 cycles, both arms
Exp arm: durvalumab 1500 mg monthly x12 infusions

details: 🔍 Median age 67, 68% male, 77% SCC, 70% node-positive
⚠️ TRAEs higher with durvalumab; G≥3 AE rates similar. No AE numbers in source
⚠️ Sized for HR 0.55: the 95% CI (0.55-1.49) cannot exclude a smaller benefit
⚠️ No local control or pattern-of-failure data reported in abstract
🔗 Same question as KUNLUN (durvalumab + dCRT, ESCC); contrasts with CheckMate 577 adjuvant nivolumab after trimodality

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase II with centrally reviewed primary cleanly missed; reaffirms dCRT alone. Small, powered only for a large effect (HR 0.55), so a modest benefit is not excluded.
verdict.audience: Non-metastatic locally advanced esophageal SCC or unresectable ADK, PS ≤1

studies.significance: The RT backbone was a modern IMRT 50 Gy/25 fx with FOLFOX, and centrally reviewed PFS was identical at 12 mo (48.6% vs 48.9%), so the null is not explained by an outdated RT platform. No local control or in-field failure data were reported, leaving open whether durvalumab changes the locoregional failure pattern that dominates after dCRT.
studies.monday_clinic: In non-metastatic locally advanced esophageal SCC or unresectable adenocarcinoma treated with definitive FOLFOX-based CRT, this does not support adding durvalumab; it does not speak to adjuvant IO after neoadjuvant CRT and resection.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Open-label, comparative, multicentric **randomized phase II**; 112 pts randomized May 2019 to May 2024 across 13 French sites. Stratified by stage, histology and center. Analysis after **24-month follow-up**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Age ≥18, WHO PS ≤1, **non-metastatic locally advanced SCC or unresectable adenocarcinoma**. Median age 67, 68% male, 77% SCC, 70% with nodal extension.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **IMRT 50 Gy in 25 daily fractions** over 5 weeks in both arms, with 6 cycles of FOLFOX (oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2, leucovorin 200 mg/m2, 5-FU 400 mg/m2 bolus then 2400 mg/m2 over 46 h).

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Experimental arm added **durvalumab 1500 mg monthly for 12 infusions** to SoC CRT. Timing of the first dose relative to RT is not stated in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** centrally reviewed PFS (cPFS). Secondary: OS, PFS, safety. 74 cPFS events required to detect **HR 0.55** with 90% power at 10% one-sided alpha.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Treatment-related AEs were **higher with durvalumab**; grade ≥3 AE rates were similar between arms. No new safety signal. Per-arm rates not given in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Asks the same question as KUNLUN (durvalumab with dCRT in ESCC) and differs from CheckMate 577, where IO is given adjuvantly after neoadjuvant CRT and resection. ARION adds a FOLFOX backbone and an adenocarcinoma minority to that evidence.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents non-metastatic locally advanced esophageal SCC or unresectable adenocarcinoma, PS ≤1, receiving 50 Gy/25 fx IMRT with FOLFOX. Does not represent pts going to resection after neoadjuvant CRT or those with metastatic disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Events per arm and median PFS not reported. No local control or failure-pattern data. The **adenocarcinoma subset (23%)** is too small to read on its own, and the 10% one-sided alpha is permissive even for a phase II.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Adding PD-L1 blockade to FOLFOX-based dCRT produced **no PFS or OS signal** at 24 months. Longer follow-up and predictive factors are pending, so a biomarker-selected benefit is not ruled out, but an unselected population shows nothing.

studies.interpretation:
The theory behind ARION was the same one behind PACIFIC in lung: chemoradiation makes tumors more immunogenic, so consolidating with PD-L1 blockade should turn a response that usually doesn't last into a lasting one. In the esophagus that has not worked. The centrally reviewed 12-month PFS rates in the two arms are practically the same (48.6% and 48.9%). Investigator-assessed PFS and OS point the same way, with hazard ratios of 0.92 and 0.99. When three endpoints agree this closely, chance imbalance in a small trial is a weak explanation for the null.

What the trial cannot do is rule out a modest effect. It was sized to find a hazard ratio of 0.55, which is a large effect for an IO add-on, at a permissive 10% one-sided alpha. The 95% interval on cPFS reaches 0.55 at its lower end, so the data still allow a benefit as large as the one the trial was designed to find. They also allow harm. The fairest reading is that ARION found no evidence of the large benefit it was built to detect, and that the smaller benefit seen in other IO settings is still open. The OS rates at 12 months (75.1% and 67.9%) are the one place the arms look different, but the adjusted HR of 0.99 suggests that difference does not hold over the full curve. It should not be read as a survival signal.

The backbone matters for how far the result transfers. Both arms got IMRT 50 Gy in 25 fractions with FOLFOX, which matches the modern European dCRT standard more closely than the older cisplatin-based regimens. That makes it hard to argue the null reflects an outdated RT platform. It also means the result says nothing about IO given after neoadjuvant CRT and resection, the CheckMate 577 setting, where the biology (residual disease after surgery) and the timing differ. The KUNLUN program asked the durvalumab-plus-dCRT question in ESCC, and the field will read ARION alongside it. ARION's contribution is a mixed population with about a quarter adenocarcinoma, though that subset is too small to say anything on its own.

For a radiation oncologist, the bigger gap is the endpoint. After definitive CRT for esophageal cancer, most failures are locoregional, and an IO effect on in-field control could plausibly show up in local control before it shows up in PFS. The abstract reports no local control, no patterns of failure, and no breakdown of where progression happened. Durvalumab start timing relative to RT is also not stated, which matters because concurrent and sequential exposure may differ. Until those data are presented, ARION supports keeping dCRT alone as the backbone for unselected pts. It does not close the question for biomarker-selected subsets, and the investigators say predictive factors will be reported.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: With a 50 Gy/25 fx IMRT + FOLFOX backbone, adding durvalumab left 12-mo cPFS unchanged (48.6% vs 48.9%). No local control or pattern-of-failure endpoints were reported, so whether IO alters in-field failure after dCRT is still unknown.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Durvalumab 1500 mg monthly x12 with FOLFOX-based dCRT gave no PFS or OS gain (OS HR 0.99) and more TRAEs. The source flags predictive factors as still to be presented; no biomarker selection was reported in this analysis.

open_questions: Does durvalumab alter locoregional failure pattern after dCRT?
Predictive biomarker for IO benefit with esophageal dCRT
Benefit with PD-L1-selected or adenocarcinoma subsets

studies.name: AGITG MASTERPLAN
studies.tldr: 12mth LRR 20.2% vs 52.0% (p=0.022) adding SBRT 40Gy/5fx to induction CT; mOS 22.0 vs 14.0mo (p=0.006), G3+ toxicity similar.
details: 🔍 Randomised phase II, 2:1, CT+SBRT vs CT alone, 14 sites, 75 enrolled (1 ineligible)
🔍 Mixed population: 48 potentially operable (high-risk operable + BRPC), 26 inoperable (LAPC / medically inoperable)
💊 CT clinician choice: mFOLFIRINOX 90% (I) vs 92% (C); gem/nab-paclitaxel the rest
🔍 SBRT 40Gy/5fx, fiducial guidance, real-time RT QA; central radiology review of staging

details.text: 📊 Efficacy and toxicity, CT+SBRT (I, n=49) vs CT alone (C, n=25)

details: ⚠️ Only 39/49 (80%) of the SBRT arm commenced SBRT; analysis population not stated
⚠️ IPC LRR benefit not significant (p=0.16); only 26 IPC pts
⚠️ Sex imbalance: 72% male (C) vs 51% (I), p=0.08
⚠️ OS is secondary; control arm only n=25, follow-up duration not reported in source
🔗 Diverges from Alliance A021501, where adding SBRT to mFOLFIRINOX in BRPC did not improve outcomes

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase II, 1° LRR met, but N=74 with control n=25, follow-up unreported, OS secondary. Diverges from A021501; needs phase III replication.
verdict.audience: High-risk operable, borderline resectable or locally advanced pancreatic cancer

studies.significance: Technique gates transfer: 40Gy/5fx with fiducial guidance and real-time RT QA, inside a 3mth induction CT window. Only 39 of 49 (80%) commenced SBRT, yet 12mth LRR still fell to 20.2% vs 52.0%. R0 (>1mm) 62% vs 40% (p=0.44) hints at a margin effect the trial was not powered to test.
studies.monday_clinic: In BRPC or high-risk operable pancreatic cancer on induction mFOLFIRINOX, this supports discussing added SBRT for locoregional control, ideally on trial; it does not settle LAPC or medically inoperable disease, where the LRR difference was not significant.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomised phase II**, 2:1 to 3mths CT+SBRT vs 3mths CT alone, 14 sites. 75 enrolled, 1 ineligible; 49 investigational, 25 control. Staging per AGITG guidelines with central radiology review.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Operable with **≥1 high-risk feature** (>4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, or node positive), BRPC, or LAPC. Grouped as potentially operable (POPC, n=48) vs inoperable (IPC, n=26). Median age 65-66; cN0 71% (I) vs 60% (C).

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: CT by clinician choice, **mFOLFIRINOX in 90% vs 92%**, gem/nab-paclitaxel otherwise. Resected pts got 3mths adjuvant CT; unresectable pts continued CT a further 3mths.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 40Gy in 5 fractions** with fiducial marker guidance and real-time RT quality assurance. SBRT commenced in **39 (80%)** of the investigational arm. Timing relative to CT within the 3mth window not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: 12mth LRR.** Secondary: resection rate, margin status, CTCAE v5.0 toxicity, PFS, OS.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: LRR benefit held in **POPC (p=0.031)** but did not reach significance in IPC (p=0.16). PFS and OS both favored SBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3+ toxicity **70.2% vs 64.0%, p=0.27**; no added toxicity signal from SBRT in this sample.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Alliance A021501 added SBRT to mFOLFIRINOX in BRPC and the SBRT arm did not improve outcomes. LAP07 tested conventional chemoradiation vs continued chemo in LAPC without an OS benefit. MASTERPLAN is the first randomised signal in this setting with local recurrence as the primary endpoint.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents high-risk operable and borderline resectable pancreatic cancer on induction mFOLFIRINOX. Does not represent LAPC or medically inoperable disease, where the LRR difference was not significant.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: 20% of the SBRT arm never started SBRT, and the analysis population is not stated. Sex imbalance (72% vs 51% male) and clinician-choice CT add noise to a 25-pt control arm.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A lower LRR is the endpoint SBRT should move, so the primary result is biologically coherent. The OS gap is larger than LRR control alone would usually explain in a disease driven by distant failure, which argues for replication before attributing survival to SBRT.

studies.interpretation:
The case for pancreatic RT has rested on an awkward split: locoregional failure is common and morbid, yet randomised trials of RT added to chemotherapy have not shown a survival gain. LAP07 tested conventional chemoradiation after induction chemo in LAPC and found no OS benefit, and in the borderline resectable setting the Alliance A021501 SBRT arm did not improve on mFOLFIRINOX alone. MASTERPLAN breaks from that pattern on two counts. It chose local recurrence as its primary endpoint, the outcome SBRT is mechanistically positioned to change, and it reports an OS difference (22.0 vs 14.0 mths, p=0.006) that the prior trials did not.

The LRR result is the more credible of the two. A drop from 52.0% to 20.2% at 12 months is large, consistent across the potentially operable subgroup (19.7% vs 52.9%), and directionally similar in the inoperable subgroup (21.4% vs 50.0%) where 26 pts simply cannot power a p-value below 0.16. The technique is modern and well controlled: 40Gy in 5 fractions, fiducial guidance, real-time QA, central radiology review. That matters for transfer, because a reader delivering SBRT without fiducials or motion management is not replicating this intervention.

The OS signal deserves more caution than the abstract's conclusion gives it. Pancreatic cancer mortality is driven mainly by distant failure, so an eight-month median OS gain from a local therapy implies either that locoregional control has more downstream effect than generally assumed, or that something else differs between arms. A control arm of 25 is small enough for chance imbalance to move a median, and there is a visible one: 72% vs 51% male. CT was clinician choice, follow-up duration is not reported, and the analysis population is not stated even though 20% of the SBRT arm never received SBRT. If the analysis is ITT, the non-delivery would dilute the effect and makes the LRR result more impressive; if it is per-protocol, it introduces selection toward fitter pts.

The surgical data neither confirm nor refute a mechanism. Resection (68% vs 59%) and R0 above 1mm (62% vs 40%) both lean toward SBRT, but neither is significant in 48 POPC pts. A margin effect is a plausible link between SBRT and survival in the resected subset, yet the trial was not built to test it.

What this changes is the framing of the A021501 result rather than practice outright. A reader who took that trial as evidence that SBRT adds nothing to modern induction chemo now has randomised data pointing the other way, with a stronger local-control design. What it does not settle is whether the OS benefit is real, whether the inoperable subgroup benefits, and how SBRT should be timed within induction. A phase III with OS as primary endpoint, stratified by operability, is the obvious next step.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 40Gy/5fx with fiducials and real-time QA cut 12mth LRR to 20.2% vs 52.0%, even with only 80% of the arm commencing SBRT. This reopens SBRT after induction CT in BRPC, against the A021501 read, but only for a comparably controlled technique.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: SBRT was layered onto clinician-choice induction (mFOLFIRINOX ~90%) without a G3+ toxicity penalty (70.2% vs 64.0%, p=0.27). The PFS 11.9 vs 6.3 mths and OS 22.0 vs 14.0 mths gaps sit on a 25-pt control arm, so the systemic sequence stays unchanged pending replication.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: In potentially operable pts, resection 68% vs 59% and R0 (>1mm) 62% vs 40% leaned toward SBRT, neither significant (p=0.54, p=0.44). SBRT did not compromise operability in this sample, but a margin benefit remains unproven.

open_questions: Does the OS signal replicate in a phase III?
Does SBRT benefit LAPC or medically inoperable disease?

studies.name: KEYNOTE-975
studies.tldr: EFS 15.2 vs 14.7 mo, HR 0.97 (0.77–1.23) in PD-L1 CPS ≥10; adding pembro to dCRT failed its primary endpoint, and the trial was stopped.
details: 🔍 Phase 3, randomized 1:1, double-blind, placebo-controlled, international; N=703 (349 pembro vs 354 placebo)
🔍 Unresectable, previously untreated locally advanced ESCC, EAC or GEJ; ECOG 0-1; dCRT-eligible

subdetails: dCRT: investigator-choice FP + 50 or 60 Gy, or FOLFOX + 50 Gy
Pembro 200 mg q3w x8 cycles → 400 mg q6w x5 cycles, vs matching placebo

details.text: 📊 Dual primary endpoints in PD-L1 CPS ≥10 (2nd interim analysis, median f/u 47.1 mo)

details: 📐 EFS in CPS ≥10 not met, so hierarchical testing stopped; no formal EFS readout in CPS ≥1 or ITT

details.text: ⚠️ Safety: toxicity higher with pembro + dCRT

details: ⚠️ Null even in the CPS ≥10 enriched population, which is where an IO signal should have been easiest to find
⚠️ RT dose (50 vs 60 Gy) and histology subgroups not reported in source; local control and patterns of failure not reported
🔗 Concurrent-with-dCRT IO, unlike the consolidation (PACIFIC, NSCLC) or post-resection adjuvant (CheckMate 577) settings

verdict.rationale: Double-blind phase 3 that missed its prespecified primary in the enriched CPS ≥10 group and was stopped. Supports dCRT alone as standard, with no IO added.
verdict.audience: Unresectable locally advanced ESCC/EAC/GEJ, untreated, ECOG 0-1

studies.significance: The RT backbone was heterogeneous (50 or 60 Gy with FP, or 50 Gy with FOLFOX), and the source gives no dose-stratified or local-control readout. The trial therefore cannot say whether IO interacts with RT dose. It does settle the concurrent question for CPS ≥10, where fatal AEs ran 13% vs 10% with no EFS gain.
studies.monday_clinic: In an unresectable esophageal or GEJ cancer pt planned for dCRT, even with PD-L1 CPS ≥10, this does not support adding concurrent pembro. It does not address consolidation-only IO after dCRT or the resectable trimodality pathway.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International **randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3**, 1:1, N=703. Results are from the **second interim analysis** (data cutoff January 21, 2026, median follow-up 47.1 mo). The study was **stopped** after this readout.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Previously untreated, unresectable** locally advanced ESCC, EAC or GEJ cancer. ECOG 0-1, ineligible for curative surgery but suitable for dCRT.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Pembro 200 mg q3w for 8 cycles, then 400 mg q6w for 5 cycles, vs matching placebo, both given with dCRT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Investigator-selected: **FP with 50 or 60 Gy**, or **FOLFOX with 50 Gy**. The source does not give fractionation, target volume or dose-stratified outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Dual primary:** investigator-assessed EFS and OS, tested in CPS ≥10, CPS ≥1 and the overall population. Because EFS in CPS ≥10 failed, formal testing of the remaining hypotheses did not proceed.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Grade ≥3 AEs in 100% of both arms. **Fatal AEs 13% vs 10%** and discontinuation 34% vs 27%, both higher with pembro.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: In NSCLC (PACIFIC) and resected esophageal cancer after neoadjuvant CRT (CheckMate 577), IO was given after RT, not concurrently. KEYNOTE-975 tested concurrent-plus-maintenance pembro in definitive esophageal CRT and found **no benefit**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents unresectable, untreated locally advanced esophageal/GEJ cancer, PD-L1 CPS ≥10, receiving dCRT. Does not represent resectable disease on a trimodality pathway or consolidation-only IO after completed dCRT.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Biomarker enrichment did not open a window for concurrent pembro, and OS was flat at HR 1.00. Whether timing, histology or RT dose hides a benefit cannot be judged from the reported data.

studies.interpretation:
KEYNOTE-975 is a clean negative. Randomization, a double-blind placebo control, a prespecified hierarchy and 47.1 months of median follow-up leave little room to blame the design. The hierarchy started in the PD-L1 CPS ≥10 population, the group most likely to respond to checkpoint inhibition. The EFS hazard ratio there was 0.97 and the OS hazard ratio 1.00. When the enriched stratum shows nothing, there is little reason to expect the CPS ≥1 or all-comer populations to do better, even though they were never formally tested. Stopping the study after the second interim analysis is consistent with that read.

The result fits poorly with how checkpoint inhibitors earned their place around radiation elsewhere. PACIFIC in stage III NSCLC and CheckMate 577 in resected esophageal cancer after neoadjuvant chemoradiation both gave IO after the radiation course, in pts who had already shown they could tolerate it. KEYNOTE-975 started pembro alongside dCRT and continued it as maintenance. A plausible hypothesis is that concurrent delivery during an intensely lymphotoxic course, in pts selected for being unresectable, is the wrong window. The trial cannot test that idea. It does show that concurrent-plus-maintenance pembro, as given here, does not work, and that its negative result should not be read across to a consolidation-only design.

The toxicity data deserve more weight than the efficacy table. Grade ≥3 AEs reached 100% in both arms, which suggests either a very inclusive grading definition or a population at the limit of what it can tolerate. On that background, pembro added deaths (fatal AEs 13% vs 10%) and discontinuations (34% vs 27%) without any EFS gain. A reader hoping for a small, underpowered benefit hidden in the noise should note that the safety signal points the other way.

For a radiation oncologist, the main gaps are on the radiation side. The RT dose was left to the investigator: 50 or 60 Gy with FP, or 50 Gy with FOLFOX. The source reports no local control, in-field versus out-of-field failure, or dose-stratified outcomes. So the trial cannot say whether pembro changes the dose question, or whether a local-regional signal sits beneath a null EFS. Histology is a similar blind spot. The trial pooled ESCC with adenocarcinoma of the esophagus and GEJ, two diseases with different biology and different sensitivity to immunotherapy, and the source reports no split by histology.

For the result to be wrong, a benefit would have to be confined to a subgroup that the hierarchy never reached, or offset by toxicity-driven early deaths that a longer, more selective design could avoid. Neither is excluded, but neither is supported by the source. The practical read is that dCRT without concurrent IO remains the backbone for unresectable disease. The open question moves to sequencing (consolidation after dCRT) and to better pt selection, not to repeating this design.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Investigators chose the dCRT backbone (50 or 60 Gy with FP, or 50 Gy with FOLFOX), and the source reports no local control, pattern-of-failure or dose subgroup data. For CPS ≥10 unresectable disease, the RT plan stays as it is, with no concurrent pembro.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: PD-L1 CPS ≥10 enrichment did not rescue concurrent pembro: EFS HR 0.97 and OS HR 1.00. Discontinuation for AEs was 34% vs 27%. For dCRT candidates, concurrent-plus-maintenance pembro as given here has no supporting EFS data.

open_questions: Would consolidation-only IO after dCRT succeed where concurrent pembro failed?
Does benefit differ by histology (ESCC vs adenocarcinoma) or RT dose?
What drove the higher fatal AE rate with pembro plus dCRT?

papers.title: Randomised phase II study of mFOLFIRINOX ± SBRT in patients with high risk, borderline resectable or locally advanced pancreatic cancer: Results of the AGITG MASTERPLAN trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3136RO · Rapid oral 1: Gastrointestinal tumour, upper digestive · 2026-10-23 · presented by Andrew Oar (Southport, Australia)

Background: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) delivers high-dose, precision radiotherapy (RT). Despite advances in chemotherapy (CT) for pancreatic cancer (PC), locoregional recurrences (LRR) are frequent and contribute to morbidity/mortality.
Methods: Eligible pts had operable disease with ≥1 high risk feature (>4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, or node positive), or BRPC, or LAPC. High-risk operable and BRPC pts were classified as potentially operable PC (POPC), while LAPC/medically inoperable pts as inoperable PC (IPC). Staging followed AGITG guidelines with central radiology review. CT was clinician choice: mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel. Pts were randomised 2:1 to 3mths of CT+SBRT (I) or to 3mths CT alone (C). SBRT was 40Gy in 5 fractions with fiducial marker guidance and real time RT quality assurance. After CT±SBRT, pts were evaluated for surgery. Following resection pts received 3mths adjuvant CT. Pts unsuitable for resection, continued CT for further 3mths. The primary endpoint was 12mth LRR. Secondary endpoints included resection rate, margin status, toxicity per CTCAE (v5.0), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS).
Results: Across 14 sites 75 pts were enrolled with 1 ineligible, including 48 POPC and 26 IPC. 12mth LRR rates were 20.2 % (95% CI: 9.9-33.2%) v 52.0% (95% CI: 30.3-69.9%) in I and C respectively (p=0.022). In POPC, 12mth LRR rates were 19.7% (95% CI: 7.8–35.6) (I) v 52.9% (95% CI: 25.9–74.1) (C) (p=0.031), and in IPC 21.4% (95% CI: 4.8–45.8) (I) v 50.0% (95% CI: 11.4-80.2) (C) (p=0.16). Overall Grade 3+ toxicity occurred in 70.2% (I) and 64.0% (C) (p=0.27). Median PFS was 11.9 v 6.3 mths (p=0.002) and median OS 22.0 v 14.0 mths (p=0.006) in I and C, respectively. Conclusions: SBRT improved LRR and PFS without additional toxicity. A significant OS signal was observed in this cohort. Further research to optimise the role of SBRT is required.

papers.title: A new fast-acting treatment option for painful bone metastases: A confirmatory trial of palliative arterial embolization assessing immediate efficacy and safety (PALEM Trial)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3087RO · Rapid oral: Supportive and palliative care · 2026-10-25 · presented by Yasunori Arai (Kashiwa, Japan)

Background: Painful bone metastases impair quality of life in patients with cancer, yet few options beyond analgesics provide relief within days. Palliative arterial embolization may enable rapid pain control by embolizing tumor-feeding vessels. We prospectively evaluated its immediate efficacy and safety.
Methods: The PALEM trial was a multicenter, single-arm, prospective confirmatory hypothesis-assessment study conducted under national palliative trial standards (J-SUPPORT policy). This protocol has been published. Eligible patients [on analgesics; Pain score ≥5; radiotherapy (RT)-ineligible or ≥8 weeks after prior RT] underwent embolization for the most painful lesion using microsphere, without anticancer drugs. The co-primary endpoints were immediate efficacy and safety. Immediate efficacy was defined by international consensus criteria for palliative RT trials, incorporating pain scores and daily morphine-equivalent doses. Pain score (Brief pain Inventory - short form item 3) was assessed at 72 h. Efficasy was defined as (a) reduced pain score with reduced opioid dose, (b) reduced pain score with unchanged opioid dose, or (c) unchanged pain score with reduced opioid dose. Immediate efficacy was evaluated by testing whether the efficasy rate exceeded 26% (one-sided α=0.025, 1−β=0.9), assuming a 40% response. Safety was defined as the incidence, through day 14, of embolization-related adverse events (any Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Event grade ≥4 event or grade ≥3 central nervous system necrosis). We tested whether the adverse event rate was <15% (one-sided α=0.025, 1−β=0.9). Overall success required both immediate efficacy and safety criteria be met.
Results: A total of 120 patients were enrolled. Immediate efficacy was achieved for 62 of 118 evaluable patients, yielding a 52.5% pain-relief rate (95% CI, 43.1–61.8%). The safety analysis set included 119 patients; no primary safety events occurred (95% CI, 0.0–3.1%). The trial met both primary endpoints.
Conclusions: The PALEM trial confirmed palliative arterial embolization as a valid treatment for painful bone metastases, providing immediate pain relief with acceptable safety.
Clinical trial identification: UMIN-CTR ID: UMIN000040794 release date: 2020/07/01.

papers.title: MRI-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound versus external beam radiotherapy for painful bone metastases: The FURTHER RCT
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3084O · Proffered paper: Supportive and palliative care · 2026-10-26 · presented by Manon Braat (Utrecht, Netherlands) · NCT04307914

Background: External beam radiotherapy (EBRT) is the standard of treatment for patients with painful bone metastases. Its effect takes 4-6 weeks to occur and 70% of patients achieve pain response. MRI-guided High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (MR-HIFU) is proposed as alternative or addition to EBRT. The multicenter FURTHER RCT investigated whether MR-HIFU, with or without EBRT, induces earlier and better pain response in patients with painful bone metastases.
Methods: Patients were enrolled between 2020-2025 in six European hospitals. Patients were adults with good/reasonable performance, painful (NRS ≥ 4) non-spinal bone metastases, eligible for EBRT and MR-HIFU. Patients with life expectancy <3 months, (impending) fracture, or curative treatment intent were excluded. Patients were 1:1:1 randomized to MR-HIFU, EBRT, or the combination (EBRT followed by MR-Hifu within one week). Primary endpoint was pain response two weeks following start of treatment based on pain score and opioid use as collected by the Brief Pain Inventory. Secondary endpoints included pain scores and pain response over the first three months.
Results: Despite 2 year project extention, the target sample size of 129 patients was not reached due COVID-19 and lower-than-expected MR-HIFU eligibility. 69 patients were randomized to MR-HIFU (n=22), combination treatment (n=23) and EBRT (n=24). Two weeks after the start of treatment, pain response was higher for MR-HIFU (with or without EBRT) than for EBRT; the difference was not statistically significant (50% vs. 38%, p = 0.41). In the first 2 weeks following start of treatment, pain scores dropped 2.3 points in the EBRT arm, 3.7 points in the combination arm, and 3.6 points in the MR- HIFU arm. Between 1-6 weeks following start of treatment, pain response increased from 35% to 47% for EBRT, from 26% to 81% for the combination treatment and from 47% to 50% for MR- HIFU.
Conclusions: MR- HIFU is effective for palliation of painful bone metastases and can be considered in patients for whom EBRT is no (longer an) option. Combining EBRT with MR- HIFU may lead to a higher pain response than current standard treatment. Bayesian analyses to mitigate the study's low power and improve its interpretability will be presented at ESMO.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04307914.

papers.title: Durvalumab plus definitive chemoradiotherapy versus definitive chemoradiotherapy in patients with locally advanced esophagus carcinoma: ARION PRODIGE 67 randomized phase 2 trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 2879RO · Rapid oral 1: Gastrointestinal tumour, upper digestive · 2026-10-23 · presented by Marie-Anouchka Modesto (Toulouse, France) · NCT03777813

Background: In locally advanced or unresectable esophageal cancer, definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is the standard of care (SoC) combining radiotherapy with platinum-based chemotherapy, resulting in a 2-year disease-free survival of 25%, which remains an unmet medical need. As immune checkpoint inhibitors increase survival in the metastatic setting, a multicentric, this open-label, comparative phase II ARION trial was designed to assess efficacy and safety of PD1/PDL1 blockade by durvalumab (D) added to SoC.
Methods: Patients (pts) ≥18 years old, WHO performance status ≤1, non-metastatic, locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) or unresectable adenocarcinoma (ADK), (stratified by tumor stage, histology, centers) were randomized between arm A with 12 monthly 1500 mg (D) infusions added to SoC (IMRT 50 Gy/25 daily fractions over 5 weeks) and 6 cycles of FOLFOX regimen: oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2, Leucovorin 200 mg/m2, 5-FU 400 mg/m2 bolus then continuous 2400 mg/m2 over 46 h) or arm B (SoC). Primary endpoint was centrally reviewed progression-free survival (cPFS). Overall survival (OS), PFS and safety were secondary endpoints. 74 cPFS events were required to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.55 with 90% power (10% one-sided alpha).
Results: Between May 2019 and May 2024, 112 pts were randomized (Arm A: SoC + D, n=58 / Arm B: SoC, n=54) in 13 French sites. Analysis was performed after a 24-month follow-up. Median age was 67 years, 68% were male, 77% were SCC, 70% had nodal extension. There was no significant difference between arms for cPFS, PFS and OS (table). Treatment-related adverse events (AE) were higher in arm A. Grade ≥ 3 AE rates were similar in both arms. Table: 2879RO Arm A (exp) 12-month rate [95%CI] Arm B (SoC) 12-month rate [95%CI] Adjusted HR* [95%CI] [80%CI] 1-sided p-value cPFS 48.6% [34.6; 61.3] 48.9% [34.7; 61.7] 0.91 [0.55; 1.49] [0.66; 1.25] 0.351 PFS 50.1% [36.2; 62.5] 48.1% [33.7; 61.2] 0.92 [0.56; 1.50] [0.67; 1.27] 0.369 OS 75.1% [61.6; 84.4] 67.9% [53.6; 78.7] 0.99 [0.59; 1.68] [0.70; 1.40] 0.489 *for Histological subtype, Stage
Conclusions: In this indication, Durvalumab with CRT compared to SoC did not improve PFS. There was no new safety signal. Longer survival, follow-up and predictive factors for treatment efficacy will be presented.
